name: Maryland bridge
lead: A Maryland bridge, also called a resin-bonded or adhesive bridge, replaces a missing tooth with a pontic that has metal or ceramic 'wings' bonded to the etched enamel of neighbouring teeth, requiring little or no preparation of them.[1][2] Its name is noted on Wikipedia, which has no history section for it.[1]

It is discussed in the appearance context mainly as a conservative way to replace a missing front tooth. Wikipedia states that debonding is the main failure concern, that cantilever single-retainer designs have fewer complications than designs bonded on both sides, and that contraindications include bruxism, mobile teeth and nickel allergy.[1]

paras: Designs include fixed-fixed, fixed-movable and cantilever types; the cantilever is the most tooth-conserving, preferred for single front teeth and easy to clean, but its small bonding area gives limited retention.[1] Laboratory work compared retainer shapes such as grooves and pins for resistance to displacement.[3]
Indications include single-tooth replacement with sound, unrestored neighbours, stable gum health, and patients unsuited to implants.[1] A debonded wing can allow decay to develop beneath it.[1]

A 1988 clinical review covered the etched cast resin-bonded bridge,[2] and clinical-technique papers reported long-term results.[4][5] Registered randomized trials have studied cantilever resin-bonded bridges for molars, zirconia and lithium-disilicate versions, and no-preparation designs.[6][7][8][9]

card.summary: A winged bridge glued to neighbouring teeth to replace a missing tooth with little drilling; debonding is the usual failure.
card.note: Not suited to grinders, mobile teeth or nickel allergy.

quick.overview:
A Maryland bridge replaces a missing tooth, often a front tooth, using a false tooth with wings glued behind the adjacent teeth.

It preserves more natural tooth than a conventional bridge because little preparation is needed.
quick.mechanism: The wings are bonded to acid-etched enamel on the lingual surface of neighbouring teeth, holding the pontic in the gap.
quick.risks: Debonding is the main concern and can let decay start under a loose wing; contraindications include grinding, mobile teeth and nickel allergy.
